opus-5.5.text:
I think of the boundaries of intelligence quite broadly, maybe more broadly than a lot of people in our field would. For a long time, especially with the success of large language models, there's been a tendency to equate intelligence with language: if a system can talk fluently, reason in text, solve math problems, write code, then we say it's intelligent. And that's certainly an important part of it. But I don't think language is the whole story, and I'm not even sure it's the foundation.

If you look at the natural world, intelligence existed long before language. Animals perceive, they navigate, they predict what will happen next in their environment, they manipulate objects, they learn from experience. A cat jumping onto a table is solving a very hard problem in physics and perception and motor control, and it doesn't need a single word to do it. So to me, a big part of intelligence is grounded in perception and in understanding the physical world: building some kind of internal model of how things work, how they move, what causes what.

That's why I care so much about vision and about what people now call world models. Vision is our richest channel to reality. Language is, in a sense, a highly compressed, human-made abstraction on top of that experience. It's incredibly powerful, but it's also lossy. If we only train on text, we inherit the knowledge humans have already written down, but we might miss the kind of intuitive, embodied understanding that isn't easily verbalized.

So when I think about the boundary, I'd include perception, prediction, reasoning, planning, acting in the world, and also learning continually and adapting to new situations. And I'd add something like curiosity, the drive to explore and form new representations, rather than just retrieving or recombining what's already there.

I'd also say the boundary isn't fixed. Every time we build a system that does something we thought required intelligence, we tend to move the goalposts. Some people find that frustrating, but I think it's actually healthy. It shows that our understanding of intelligence is evolving along with the technology. So I see it less as a line to cross and more as a space we're still mapping, and right now I feel we've explored the language corner of that space pretty thoroughly, while the parts connected to the physical, visual, embodied world are still wide open.

r001.rationale: The response says animals perceive and navigate, but it does not connect the breadth of intelligence to differences in sensory capacities across animal species.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I try to understand it quite broadly, honestly broader than the way most of us in the field talk about it day to day.

When people say "intelligence" in AI right now, they usually mean something very specific: can a model answer hard math questions, can it write code, can it pass exams. That's a language-centric, almost test-centric view. And I understand why it dominates, because language is where we've made the most dramatic progress, and language is how we communicate, so it's the easiest thing to measure and the easiest thing to be impressed by.

But if you step back and look at intelligence as it actually exists in the world, language is a very late and very thin layer. A dog doesn't have language, a two-year-old barely has language, but they understand that objects persist when you can't see them, they understand that if you push something it moves, they can navigate a room, they can predict what happens next. That's intelligence. It's just not the kind that shows up on a benchmark.

So for me the boundary is roughly: anything that builds an internal model of the world and uses it to perceive, predict, and act. Language is one way to compress and transmit that model, and it's a powerful one, but it's not the model itself. A lot of what humans know we never put into words. That's why I spend so much of my time on vision and on representation learning. I think the visual, physical, spatial side of intelligence is the part we have barely touched, and it's the part that will ultimately decide whether these systems can operate in the real world rather than only in a chat window.

I'd also say the boundary isn't fixed. Every time we build something that works, we tend to redefine intelligence to exclude it. Chess used to be intelligence, then it wasn't. Translation used to be, then it wasn't. So I try not to draw the line too firmly. I'd rather hold a working definition that's wide enough to include things we can't yet measure, and then let the research tell us where the actual edges are.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence extends beyond language and gives a dog as an example, but it does not connect its breadth to differences in sensory capacities across animal species.

astra-6.text:
I think the first difficulty is that we don’t really know where the boundaries are. We recognize intelligence through things we can observe—learning, reasoning, adapting—but those are also shaped by the tests we choose. If we define intelligence by what humans do well, we may miss forms of intelligence that work very differently.

For me, a useful way to approach it is to ask: can a system take what it has learned and use it in a situation it hasn’t encountered before? That gets at something deeper than performing well on a particular task. But even then, intelligence probably isn’t a single scale. A system can be extraordinarily capable in one setting and surprisingly brittle in another.

So I would keep the definition broad and be cautious about declaring a boundary. In AI research, the interesting question is often where a capability stops generalizing. What changes in the environment make the system fail? What additional experience lets it adapt? Studying those failures can tell us more about intelligence than simply showing that a model has passed another benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broad definitions, generalization, and different capabilities, but does not connect intelligence’s breadth to sensory diversity across animal species.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to think of intelligence quite broadly: the ability to learn from experience, build an understanding of the world, and use that understanding to act in unfamiliar situations. Language is one expression of that, but perception, movement, and interaction with the environment matter too.

The interesting question is whether the boundaries we see today are boundaries of intelligence itself, or simply limits of our current methods. A system can be very capable in one setting and surprisingly fragile in another. That makes me cautious about treating performance on a particular task as a complete measure of intelligence.

So I wouldn’t draw a firm boundary yet. I’d ask how well a system can adapt when the task changes, when information is incomplete, or when it has to learn something through interaction. Those situations tell us more about how general its intelligence really is.

r001.rationale: The response mentions perception and interaction with the environment, but does not connect intelligence’s breadth to the diversity of sensory capacities across animal species.
